title: PM Modi hails deepening Constitution connect, urges public engagement with its ideals
description: Modi Cites Welfare Schemes, Constitutional Amendments And Anti-Naxalism Gains, While Warning That Past Actions Weakened Freedoms And Institutional Balance
author: Our Bureau
content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has marked Constitution Day on November 26 by recalling that the document was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on this day in 1949. Modi said in an article on Wednesday that the greatness of Dr Rajendra Prasad, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar and all other members of the Constituent Assembly lay in how they drew extensively from the rich traditions and civilisational wisdom of the country to frame a modern Constitution.
The Prime Minister noted that for a nation as diverse as India — with so many faiths, languages, customs and schools of thought — it was imperative for the Constitution to resonate “far beyond the precincts of Parliament and the courts”.
Modi said “our endeavour” has been to deepen the Constitution’s connect with the “collective consciousness” of the people, especially the youth, and strengthen the spirit of unity to ensure a bright future for the country.
The Prime Minister drew attention to the fact that his government decided over a decade ago that November 26 would be marked as Constitution Day.
He said the Constitution is an inseparable part of the lives of Indians. Modi pointed to the humble circumstances in which he grew up and the struggles that were a part of everyday life. The Prime Minister said his rise from modest means to the leader of the world’s largest democracy showed how extraordinary the Constitution was.
The Prime Minister highlighted a recent World Bank report that says nearly 50 crore Indians have been moved out of poverty.
The article referred to the following welfare schemes:
- The PM Awas Yojana, under which a pucca house is provided to each beneficiary. This has ensured the constitutional promise of dignity
- The Ujjwala Yojana, under which free LPG connections have been given to women from BPL families. This has freed mothers from the hardships of a smoke-filled kitchen and furthered the ideals of equality and well-being, Modi noted
- The Ayushman Bharat scheme, which enables a poor family to access quality healthcare without the fear of debt and ensures social justice
- The MUDRA and PM-SVANidhi schemes, which offer collateral-free credit to small entrepreneurs and street vendors. These schemes have delivered economic justice, Modi said
- Digital technology and platforms like UPI have transcended all divides and given to every citizen opportunities that were once available to a privileged few, thus ensuring inclusivity.
Modi also pointed to the amendments his government had introduced, such as the 101st Amendment that ushered in the GST, the 102nd Amendment that granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes, the 103rd Amendment that provided reservation to Economically Weaker Sections.
Modi said an updated version of the Constitution is now available in all 22 languages under the Eighth Schedule, which has brought it closer to the people.
The Prime Minister said that through the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, his government had tried to bring about a fundamental shift in the criminal justice system, moving from the colonial emphasis on punishment (dand) to a citizen-centric pursuit of justice (nyay).
The Prime Minister sounded a note of caution, pointing out that there have been occasions when those entrusted with upholding the Constitution had chosen to weaken it.
The article said 2026 marked 75 years of the First Amendment in 1951, when a government that was “not popularly elected used its majority in the Provisional Parliament to restrict fundamental freedoms”. The timing of the introduction of the First Amendment, only months before India’s first general election, proved that it was intended to influence the electoral process and stifle public opposition, the article added.
Modi said 2026 also marked 50 years of the implementation of the 42nd Amendment at the height of the Emergency. The amendment curtailed judicial review and fundamentally altered the balance of institutional powers, he said.
Modi also said Article 356, used to dismiss elected state governments, was troubling. He said “one party” had the “dubious record” of imposing Article 356 close to 100 times and that “one former Prime Minister” had done so 50 times.
The Prime Minister wrote about the problem of Naxalism that had blighted several parts of the country, particularly tribal areas. He highlighted how his government eliminated Naxalism this year, ensuring that the poorest of the poor can “finally exercise” their constitutional rights without fear.
Modi drew attention to how “Dimagi Naxals” were still active and were trying to derail the country’s growth trajectory.
Modi said the journey of the Constitution would be incomplete without recognising the remarkable women who helped shape it. He said it was shameful that a legislation his government sought to bring to give women adequate representation in legislative bodies was disallowed from being passed “by the one Opposition party, once again showing its disdain for constitutional values”.
Modi sought to assure “the Nari Shakti of India” that his government would ensure that justice is done to them.

title: Three-language status quo for Class VI students after top court clarifies CBSE policy
description: CBSE Says Over 93% Of Class VI Students Have Chosen Three Languages; Court Questions Treating English As A Non-native Language And Asks Board To Reconsider Policy
author: Our Bureau
content:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday said Class VI students who had already opted for the CBSE three-language policy need not revert to the earlier two-language formula.
Through a circular dated May 15, the CBSE had made the study of two Indian languages and one foreign language compulsory for classes VI to IX from 2026-27.
Following a batch of petitions in the top court assailing the CBSE’s move, the board had revised the rule to apply only to Class VI students.
On September 28, the apex court had directed the CBSE not to make its three-language formula compulsory for Class VI pupils this year.
“Extend the same relaxation to Class VI students,” the top court had said.
On Wednesday, during the brief hearing on the matter, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana clarified that students who had already opted for the three-language policy could continue with it.
“Our direction (earlier) was that students of Class VI, if they have opted for three languages, they will continue with the three languages, and if they have not opted, don’t force them…,” the bench clarified in response to an application filed by the CBSE seeking modification of certain orders passed by the top court.
The CJI later said the bench would pass a written order clarifying the court’s position.
The CBSE had pleaded that out of 23.44 lakh Class VI students, only 4,186 had decided to stick to the two-language formula. More than 93 per cent of students have opted for the three-language formula, the board submitted.
On August 20, the bench had asked the Centre and the CBSE to consider “revisiting” the three-language policy while questioning the rationale behind classifying English as a “non-native” language.
“Rather, English, which has taken deep historical roots in the country, should be considered as an ‘indigenous’ language,” the bench had told additional solicitor-general Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre.
The new policy has come under the top court’s scrutiny after petitions were filed by students and parents challenging it as impractical and stressful, especially for Class IX students preparing for their board exams.

title: ‘No tampering’ with Sheshnag, says J&K government amid roadwork row near lake site
description: Forest Minister Says Inspection Finds No Violations, While Government Accuses PDP And BJP Of Politicising Religious Site; He Says Track Remains 200-300 Feet From Lake
author: Muzaffar Raina
content:
The Omar Abdullah government in Jammu and Kashmir on Wednesday defended the “road maintenance” work on the banks of the Sheshnag lake, saying there had been no deviation from the approved track alignment.
The ruling NC accused the Opposition PDP of trying to help the BJP in the upcoming Uttar Pradesh elections by portraying Muslims as opposed to the Amarnath pilgrimage. The blame game picked up pace with PDP chief Mehbooba Mufti accusing the Omar government of allowing a road project near the lake.
Forest and environment minister Mohammad Altaf Kaloo said a team of officials was sent to inspect the high-altitude Shesnag lake and they found no evidence of tampering or violations at the site. He accused the PDP and the BJP of politicising a religious site.
Kaloo, addressing a media conference in Pahalgam, said Omar had ordered an investigation on the first day after a video went viral on social media. He said senior officials, including the chief conservator of forests and the divisional forest officer, were called and a 12-member team led by a range officer was deputed to the spot on Tuesday. “The department told me Sheshnag is completely safe,” he said.
Kaloo said the viral video showing an excavator being used for roadwork near the alpine lake was misleading. “It (the video) shows a smaller distance, but there is a gap of 200-300 feet between the track and Sheshnag,” he said, suggesting the work was happening some distance away from the lake. “Not a particle of soil has gone into Sheshnag.” He said a 12ft track had come up in the lake’s vicinity in 2012 on the directions of the Supreme Court.

title: Inflation: How rising food prices are squeezing Indian households
description: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
description: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
author: Michael Race, Jonathan Josephs, Osmond Chia
content:
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
- Published
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.
The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.
The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.
Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.
The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.
The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".
He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".
They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.
But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.
Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.
Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.
These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.
Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.
The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.
Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.
However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.
The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.
Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.
Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.
Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.
The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.
"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.
The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.
The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.
The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.
South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.
Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.
- Trump tariffs on Asia: Which economies were hit hardest? 
  - Published1 August 2025
- China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports 
  - Published19 October
US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.
"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.
The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.
The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.
Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.
Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul
  - Published22 August

title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
description: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.
author: Zoya Mateen
content:
Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
- Published
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.
But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.
India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.
What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.
The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.
Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.
The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.
"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.
India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

title: The show is on the road: How Punjab’s political parties are gearing up for elections
description: State roads and highways turn into political stage for cycle & bus yatras as Punjab parties compete for visibility before campaigning mode shifts once candidates are announced.
author: Chitleen K Sethi
content:
Chandigarh: For Punjab opposition parties that are yet to announce their door-to-door campaigners for next year’s polls, state roads and highways have turned into a political stage, with cycle rallies, roadshows, religious yatras and bus processions in full swing.
While the Congress and BJP are already visible on the streets with their Jawani Sambhal Cycle Yatra and Samrasta Sankalp Yatra respectively, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) had planned a statewide bus yatra which was postponed in wake of the impending tie-up with the BJP (which was formally announced Tuesday). The ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on the other hand is focusing on door-to-door campaigns and localised gatherings with candidates and ticket hopefuls. AAP has already announced candidates for 71 of Punjab’s 117 assembly constituencies.
Tuesday’s announcement of the BJP-SAD alliance has added another dimension to these campaigns. With the two parties now set to contest the 2027 elections together after a six-year separation, the proposed statewide bus yatra is likely to be a combined affair. Beginning from Sri Damdama Sahib in Talwandi Sabo, the bus campaign planned to cover all 117 assembly constituencies in three phases. The first phase was to run from 10 to 22 November, while subsequent phases were expected to begin from Sri Anandpur Sahib and Sri Akal Takht Sahib in Amritsar.
“The objective is not necessarily to seek votes for individual candidates at this stage, but to ensure that the parties remain visible in political conversation, demonstrate organisational strength and build a perception of growing political momentum,” Dr Kanwalpreet Kaur, a political science professor at Chandigarh’s DAV College, told ThePrint.
Also Read: Bibi Jagir Kaur’s return to Akali Dal: Why she needs the Badals, and why the Badals need her
Congress takes the cycle route
The Congress first launched the ‘Punjab Mangda Insaaf’ yatra on a bus on 4 November in the wake of Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Insaaf’ rally in Sangrur. But it was Congress’s Jawani Sambhal Cycle Yatra, led by former chief minister and Jalandhar MP Charanjit Singh Channi, that became the party’s most visible recent campaign.
Launched from Chamkaur Sahib on 12 November in the presence of Punjab Congress in-charge Sachin Pilot, state president Pargat Singh and Leader of Opposition Partap Singh Bajwa, the first phase covered approximately 625 km across 27 constituencies before concluding at Khanna on 19 November. Around 2,000 bicycles were distributed for the campaign.
The focus was on the drug menace, unemployment and the future of Punjab’s youth. But the yatra also provided the Congress leadership an opportunity to demonstrate its organisational presence and attack the AAP government on issues of governance.
The yatra, however, also brought the Congress’s internal differences into public view. Former state Congress president and Ludhiana MP Amarinder Singh Raja Warring initially stayed away and subsequently announced his own ‘Insaaf March’ in the city on foot. He eventually joined Channi’s cycle yatra at Beeja village and cycled nearly 14 km with him to Khanna, where the campaign concluded with a public rally. Pargat Singh came on a bus for his leg of the campaign.
Former Punjab BJP president Sunil Jakhar took a dig at the Congress leaders taking out their own personal yatras. “Yesterday’s yatra belonged to Pargat Singh and Partap Singh Bajwa, while today’s yatra belongs to Channi ji. Several leaders have taken out bus rallies, while Channi ji has opted for a cycle rally. There are leaders planning to take out yatras in Defender vehicles worth Rs 2-Rs 2.5 crore each. I believe this is not a yatra but a show of strength by their own party. They do not talk about Punjab’s issues at all.”
“After years of kursi politics, the Congress has rediscovered sadak politics,” said Dr Harjeshwar Singh of the department of history at SGGS College. “The response to Channi was encouraging in semi urban areas like Samrala, Khanna, Ludhiana, Kotkapura, Amargarh and Faridkot. But in rural constituencies, the response was subdued.”
Dr Singh further said: “Warring’s march on the other hand was pitched for an urban audience. He was absent when Channi passed through Ludhiana, only to appear at Beeja on the final day to ride 14 km with him. A perfect Bollywood climax — estranged brothers riding together into the sunset.”
BJP’s Samrasta Sankalp Yatra
The BJP, has held not one but two yatras to make its presence felt.
In September, it undertook the Nasha Mukt Punjab Yatra, covering all 117 assembly constituencies and culminating in a rally addressed by Union Home Minister Amit Shah in Jalandhar. The yatra received a mixed response.
Its latest initiative, the Samrasta Sankalp Yatra, was flagged off by BJP national president Nitin Nabin near Dera Sachkhand Ballan in Jalandhar on 18 November. The nationwide 2,558-km yatra, organised to mark the 650th Prakash Purab of Guru Ravidas, has a Punjab leg covering approximately 700 km across 17 districts.
The route takes the procession through Jalandhar, Hoshiarpur, Pathankot, Gurdaspur, Amritsar, Tarn Taran, Ferozepur, Bathinda, Sangrur, Ludhiana, Ropar and Mohali before it proceeds towards Chandigarh.
The choice of Dera Sachkhand Ballan as the starting point is significant. Punjab has a Scheduled Caste population of nearly 32 percent as per 2011 Census data, and the dera has considerable influence among the Ravidassia community, particularly in the Doaba region. In Amritsar, the procession was welcomed at the Central Temple of Shri Guru Ravidas Ji in Hall Bazaar, where a religious diwan was organised.
“The emerging pattern suggests that Punjab’s election campaign is entering a phase in which political parties are competing as much for public visibility as for electoral support. This is going to remain till the candidates are announced, which is when the campaigning will shift to the micro level and individual candidates will take over,” said DAV College’s Dr Kaur, quoted earlier.
Akalis’ proposed yatra yet to hit the road
The SAD’s proposed statewide Punjab Bachao Yatra under Sukhbir Badal has been postponed twice.
The first phase was originally scheduled to begin from Takht Damdama Sahib in Talwandi Sabo on 10 November and cover 14 assembly constituencies by 22 November. It was subsequently rescheduled to 16 November before being cancelled again, with no fresh date announced.
With the much-awaited announcement of its tie-up with the BJP now made, the two parties are likely to announce joint programmes.
On the ground, the SAD has not announced its candidates, but it has asked its halka in-charges (or constituency in-charges) to not waste time and start door-to-door campaigns.
Sukhbir also simultaneously launched a statewide campaign from Gidderbaha on 6 October to collect public suggestions for the party’s 2027 manifesto. In Jalandhar, the SAD claimed to have distributed 25,000 feedback forms across four assembly constituencies.
Meanwhile, Lok Sabha MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal’s Maawan-Dhiyan Insaaf Yatra has been holding meetings with women across Punjab, focusing on the drug problem and women’s safety.
AAP moves towards constituency-level campaigning
The AAP’s move to declare candidates is reaping dividends. The party released its first list of 40 candidates on 31 October and followed it with another list of 31 on 12 November, taking the total to 71. This has allowed the candidates to hit the ground running, well ahead of the others.
In September, the party launched the Mann De Munaffe campaign, under which MLAs and party workers were assigned households to distribute the government’s four-and-a-half-year report card.
The exercise covered constituencies including Guru Har Sahai, Ferozepur Rural, Rupnagar, Ludhiana North, Amloh, Shahkot, Balachaur and Kharar. The party’s messaging has centred on free electricity, Aam Aadmi Clinics, monthly grant of Rs 1,000 to women, employment initiatives and welfare schemes.
The AAP has also announced a statewide organisational exercise involving 2.68 lakh booth committee members across 25,332 polling booths. The aim is to establish contact with voters at the polling-booth level while highlighting the government’s achievements.
The party is now preparing for its 26 November Khushhaal Punjab Maha Rally in Moga, where Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal are expected to address the gathering. The event is being projected as the formal launch of the party’s campaign for polls.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

title: The story of Yu: A Manipur rice wine rooted in meticulous tradition, now tainted by a deadly tragedy
description: Yu is being prepared as it has been for generations in almost every household of Andro village. But the deaths in Chandel and Kakching this past week expose a different reality.
author: Samridhi Tewari
content:
Imphal/Kakching/Chandel: An alcoholic sweet-and-sour aroma wafts around a quiet courtyard in Andro, a foothill village about 25 km east of Imphal in Manipur. It comes from a makeshift mud stove, a mix of woodsmoke and fermenting rice.
Yu is being prepared, as it has been for generations in almost every household of this Meitei village. The fermentation and distillation of rice produces the traditional alcoholic beverage. Andro is one of the villages known for the locally made brew.
For 55-year-old Chingakham Memcha, this has been her everyday routine for more than two decades. Beginning at 8 am and working until the sun sets, Memcha, wearing the traditional wraparound called ‘phanek’, washes rice, sets it to ferment, and quickly manages the boiling pots.
Yu is no quick-fix intoxicant or merely a side-gig. Rice wine and beer are an essential part of religious rituals and community life in Andro.
That quiet routine came to a sudden halt this past week, when 17 people died after consuming spurious liquor in the neighbouring districts of Chandel and Kakching.
According to Manipur Police sources, the victims in Chandel had purchased the liquor from Sugnu, a batch allegedly traced back to Andro. In the aftermath, police and excise officials arrested nine people from the village, registered 159 cases under the Excise Act, and launched a sweeping statewide crackdown, even as a Special Investigation Team (SIT) probes the supply chain and health officials screen hundreds of residents.
Yu is at the centre of this crackdown. How is it made? Has this age-old craft been touched by modernity? Who are the people behind it? What happened after Manipur lifted its three-decade-long prohibition in December 2023? ThePrint travelled to Andro, Sugnu and Chandel to find out.
The ‘secret’ craft of making rice wine
Located in Manipur’s Imphal East district, Andro is inhabited by the Chakpa, a Scheduled Caste sub-community of the Meiteis, and has long been preserved as a centre of indigenous Manipuri heritage and pottery.
Andro’s standout feature is a tin shed tucked into every courtyard, the ubiquitous housing for a small makeshift brewing set-up. Earthen pots, bags of rice and water stored in large buckets complete the picture.
Both brewing and pottery are strictly the domain of married women. Dressed in a baby-pink phanek and sweater, Memcha explains that she only learnt the craft after her wedding. Like most women in Andro, she does not sell her brew in the open market. “Middlemen come to our doorstep, collect the liquid, and bottle it themselves,” she tells ThePrint.
“Yu cannot be rushed. We have to wash the grains and ferment them; a single batch takes roughly two weeks,” she says.
To make eight litres of distilled rice wine, or popularly known as ‘atingba’, Memcha starts with 10 kilogrammes of local Manipuri rice, soaking it in water overnight. The next day, she separates out all the ‘yangli’, the fine husk bits that float to the surface, and kneads it with rice flour into flat, bread-like cakes called ‘humai’, the local yeast.
“The soaked rice is then steamed for three to four hours before being mixed with the humai. Covered with a cloth, the mixture is left to ferment for four days. It is topped up with cool water, and left undisturbed for another six to seven days,” she says, proudly holding two humais in her hand.
Finally, the fermented mash is transferred to a vessel for distillation, heated for four hours with a cooling pot of water balanced on top until clear drops of liquor collect inside.
For all that labour, the margins are pretty thin. Memcha spends about a thousand rupees on a single 10-kilogramme batch—half of it on rice, and the remainder on firewood and water.
Distilled yu is sold for about Rs 200 a litre, while rice beer sells for half that. A fortnight of work with fires and pots yields roughly Rs 300 in profit per batch.
“Wine is a ritual in our town, yet people outside look down on us because we make it,” Memcha says, adding that most families brew quietly behind closed doors. “Some people have used it the wrong way.”
Historically, every stage of that distillation relied on earth, not metal. Now, people have started using steel, even aluminium.
A few lanes away, sits 70-year-old Phanjoupa Khema. Her phanek is purple a striking contrast with the dark clay vessels in her shop.
Married into the village 50 years ago, Khema has spent half a century shaping clay using only a flat stone and a wooden bat to beat the mud into usable structures. A 2013 National Merit Award winner, she now trains younger women to shape pots.
Khema points out the three distinct earthen pots traditionally stacked for distillation. “There’s ‘uphu’ at the base, ‘ngangkok’ in the middle, and ‘uyasaphu’, the small vessel where the distilled wine finally collects, alongside esingzaphu to hold water,” she explains in Manipuri.
“Earlier, everything was made in earthen pots,” Khema says. “Now, aluminium and plastic have replaced them.”
Also Read: Fear & panic fuel hospital rush in Manipur amid hooch tragedy. Anxious villagers queue up for tests
Anatomy of a tragedy
The yu of Andro may well be bound by ritual, but what unfolded eight kilometres away from Sugnu in Chandel’s Chakpikarong sub-division exposes a very different reality.
The breakdown of older local supply chains after the 2023 ethnic violence, and the absence of regulation in a state shaped by prohibition birthed a shadowy network moving country-made liquor across district boundaries. “There are no licensed liquor shops in Sugnu. Instead, alcohol moves underground, sourced from valley hubs like Andro and sold discreetly out of homes and basements in Sugnu town,” a senior police officer says.
For men in Chakpikarong, where local sale is prohibited, procuring a drink meant taking a shared private jeep to Sugnu for Rs 30 to Rs 50, buying two or three plastic bottles, and carrying them back home.
The packaging looks legitimate. One plastic bottle, shaped like a mineral water bottle, carried the label Andro with ‘packaged drinking wine’ printed underneath. Another read ‘Nagola Pamjaba’, marked further as ‘premium quality’ and ‘brewed from the finest rice grains of Manipur’.
Between 17 and 19 November, residents across Chandel and Kakching districts bought these bottles in Sugnu and drank them after returning home. Within hours, the same symptoms came up: severe burning in the stomach, vomiting, and sudden, partial blindness.
Panic ripped through the villages like a tsunami making landfall as families struggled to understand what was happening.
What began as a chaotic night at the Community Health Centre in Chakpikarong and District Hospital, Chandel, quickly reached Imphal, about 100 km away, as ambulances and private vehicles brought hundreds of patients to Shija Hospital, Babina Hospital, Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences (JNIMS), and the Reginal Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS).
“On examination, doctors found symptoms consistent with methanol poisoning, prompting suspicions that they had consumed spurious liquor,” Dr Sorokhaibam Jugindra Singh, Director (Medical Services) at Shija Hospital, told ThePrint.
Across Imphal and Chandel, hospital wards ran round the clock to screen incoming patients, run toxicology and organ-function tests, and keep hundreds under 24-to-48-hour observation as the local brew mutated into a mass medical emergency.
From valley to the hills
Half-litre bottles selling for Rs 50 do not move by themselves. It’s a well-oiled machine.
According to a senior Manipur Police officer, liquor from traditional valley brewing hubs like Andro is “packed, concealed inside jeeps and four-wheelers, and taken across places like Sugnu, where middlemen who have worked the trade for years sell it out of basements”.
Police investigations into the recent deaths have pointed to specific links along that chain. Arrested suspects include Khaidem Jadumani Singh (57) of Sugnu Makha Leikai, Kangabam Surjit Singh (40) and Kangabam Ratan Singh of Sugnu Moirangthem Leikai, Khaidem Naoba Meitei (32), owner of Eikhoi Hotel in Sugnu Pamang Leikai, Ningthoujam Joykumar Singh (45) of Andro Kharam Leikai, and Sagolsem Das Singh (40) of Andro Chingdong Leikai.
“Preliminary police findings indicate Surjit Singh allegedly procured liquor from two individuals identified as Das and Nganbi of Andro, with one Dara of Sugnu Awang Leikai storing stock on Nganbi’s behalf, while Ratan Singh allegedly sourced from someone identified as Leima of Andro,” the police officer says.
Former Deputy Chief Minister and former Director General of Police Yumnam Joykumar Singh, explains the geography of the network. “Out here the districts are very small… crossing a district would be maybe about 30–40 km, not more than that,” he says. Inter-district movement of locally distilled liquor has long slipped past weak checks by the excise department as well as the police.
Joykumar, with a science background, doubts the poison began inside Andro’s distillation pots. “If the original brew made in Andro had been toxic from the start,” he said, “deaths would have been reported in Andro and Sugnu as well, and a contaminated batch at source would have killed far more people.”
Instead, he points to adulteration along the route or at the point of sale.
That movement is part of a wider smuggling system.
Police officers say that liquor is brought in from cities like Delhi by air, while security forces and state police regularly intercept bulk consignments on the highways and along the porous Manipur–Myanmar border, “where illicit drugs also move freely alongside links reaching toward China in the north and Bangladesh in the south”.
On the ground in Andro, local groups want a temporary ban on liquor sale and consumption until lab reports clarify what happened.
The policy framework
Manipur’s history with alcohol has long been shaped by prohibition, and by the gap between law and habit.
An excise department official told ThePrint that while a prohibition law was enacted in 1991, it took effect in 1994, replacing a time when licensed liquor shops existed. “Through the 1970s and 1980s, rising alcohol and drug use strained households across communities. Women led groups, the Meira Paibis, who had taken to night patrols with flaming torches in the late 1970s,” he said.
Interestingly, he added, “They pressed against addiction and bootlegging, alongside nishaband (nasha mukti) women’s groups, student bodies, and civil society organisations across Meitei, Kuki, and Naga areas.”
Yet bootleggers and habitual drinkers kept finding ways around bans enforced by women’s groups, while liquor poured in from neighbouring states whenever local supply fell short of demand.
Over the years, the state tried to carve out exceptions and rules. Amendments in 2002 allowed liquor in certain areas, and the push toward legalisation gained fresh momentum in 2022 amid debate, protests, white papers, and expert panels.
In December 2023, the government lifted prohibition in four categories of areas: Greater Imphal, hotels with 20 or more beds, district headquarters, and tourist spots. The excise official said, “This was followed by the launch of the Manipur State Beverage Corporation Limited in 2024 for government-run retail, though only six hotels and 15 retail shops have opened statewide.”
Traditionally, brewing and commercial preparation by Scheduled Caste Meitei communities in villages like Sekmai, Phayeng, and Andro, as well as traditional making among some Scheduled Tribes, have existed alongside these shifts, he said.
“The state has been working since 2024 on a Manipur Country Liquor Policy, consulting villages and studying models in states such as Goa, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, and Chhattisgarh to test, standardise, and support a craft tied to village livelihoods and women’s incomes,” the excise official added.
Enforcement, however, remains tough across departments.
Another excise official says the department runs at a thin sanctioned staff strength across 41 excise stations, even though recruitment has been notified and staff from different communities serve in their respective areas, including Kuki and Naga officers in their own community areas. “To track outside liquor, the department uses holograms to trace supply down to the last consumer and mandates UPI or card payments,” he says.
Since 17 November, officials say, over 6,000 checks have been conducted, with 159 Excise Act cases registered and 6,498 litres of illicit liquor seized, while samples were sent to Kolkata for testing and a high-level inquiry was set up.
Joykumar says the staffing crunch dates back years. When he was excise minister, he recalls, roughly 400 of 600 posts were already vacant. While an Opposition-led committee he chaired once recommended lifting prohibition on locally distilled liquor with proper controls on distillation and sales, he lost the subsequent election before those rules were put in place, and says successive governments failed to build quality checks and testing systems even after lifting the ban.
Policing priorities have also been shaped by prolonged unrest.
While Joykumar argues that policing illicit liquor is an additional task rather than the core police mandate of crime detection and investigation, he agrees that years of security and law-and-order duties have heavily taxed Manipur Police.
For now, the tragedy in Chandel and Kakching has turned a policy question into an urgent test of regulation. That question has a bottomline too: the livelihoods of the women who make yu.
Remains of the day
In the middle of conversations around the policy, police reports, arrests, and seizures, affected families continue to struggle in coping with the loss.
Kishun Hrangbung, 40, from the Naga community, cultivated plants for a living in Nungpan village in Manipur. He too drank liquor in Sugnu before returning home. He started vomiting when he reached home and struggled through the night. In the morning, he was taken to the Community Health Centre Chakpikarong, but he died within 30 minutes, his brother said.
As the family mourns Kishun’s death, their anger is palpable. “We demand answers,” they say. “Kishun, and so many other men who have died in our village, made a mistake by consuming alcohol. But, the government has to take strong action against the perpetrators. Who was responsible for making this spurious liquor? Who was responsible for selling it, and then distributing it to our people? Who will take responsibility?”
Nungpan is a Christian village with its own strict rules. Residents say the sale of liquor is prohibited. So, anyone who wants to drink has to go to Sugnu to procure it.
The ethnic violence also changed the way liquor was supplied to the village. Hrangbung Bebising, Kishun’s uncle, explains that earlier, members of the Zou community in Sugnu used to make alcohol. They would share the liquor they made and even allow people to sit in their homes and drink. Public transport was available back then, and buses also plied on the route. A few Meiteis made liquor as well.
“After 2023, the Zou community had to flee the area to Churachandpur,” he said. Bebising’s uncle has kept the two bottles Kishun brought from Sugnu. “I don’t know what to do with these two bottles that killed him. Am I to throw them away? Will the police need it? It haunts us every single day… knowing it was a bottle of alcohol that killed him,” Bebising told ThePrint.
Bebising understands that there are no licensed liquor shops in the area, but he has a question: “Why is liquor being sold with no licence then? Shouldn’t the government do something about it? You can’t ban liquor, but can you not enforce stronger regulations?”
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

title: Exclusive: China-Pakistan satellite waltz is watching every inch of India 24×7
description: This is the third exclusive by ThePrint on China's satellite surveillance of India.
author: Soumya Pillai
content:
New Delhi: China and Pakistan are building a coordinated network of satellites that could provide persistent surveillance of Indian territory. This space-based cooperation was consolidated during the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, a space surveillance report highlights.
According to a report by Bengaluru-based space surveillance startup Digantara, exclusively accessed by ThePrint, Chinese space capabilities, including satellite data, may have been used to observe Indian military installations and other strategic sites during Operation Sindoor.
One of the most significant findings points to the role of China’s high-resolution optical remote-sensing satellite, Yaogan-41, during the 88-hour military confrontation between India and Pakistan.
“Chinese Satellite Yaogan-41 offers continuous subcontinent coverage. A dual-use satellite, it tracked Indian airbases during Operation Sindoor,” the report read.
While the report pointed to the specific use of Yaogan-41 against India during Operation Sindoor, it also explained how China and Pakistan have been building a complementary network of space surveillance to ensure that not an inch of India is left unmonitored.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, Pakistan placed six satellites in orbit. Five of these—Pakistan Remote Sensing Satellite-Earth Observation 1 (PRSC-EO1), Pakistan Remote Sensing Satellite-2 (PRSS-2), HS-1, PRSC-EO2 and PRSC-EO3—were launched on Chinese rockets, in Chinese launch facilities. While all these satellites are individually placed to focus on Indian territory, they also complement the Chinese network of satellites.
The combined Earth-observation capabilities of the Pakistani and Chinese satellites give a more continuous picture of Indian military infrastructure, troop movements, border installations, airbases, naval facilities and strategic assets.
“China launched five satellites for Pakistan, enhancing ISTAR and observation of Indian assets and space monitoring capabilities,” the report read.
ISTAR is a military system that combines information gathered from satellites, drones, aircraft, radars, ground sensors and intelligence networks to give a military force a detailed picture of its adversary’s activities and capabilities.
Experts suggested that with China sharpening its space ambitions, India will need to work on its capabilities to increase its presence in space.
The Pak satellites
The Digantara report showed that the China-supported Pakistani space launches began much before 2025. Starting in 2018, satellites including PRSC-EO1, PakSat MM1, ICUBE-Q, PRSS-1 and Pak TES 1A were already eyeing Indian territory, placed in orbits complementing the existing Chinese network of satellites.
The meticulously choreographed satellite network waltz, when viewed as a whole, is designed so that as one satellite moves out of range of a particular region, another moves into position to take over, ensuring consistent coverage of the area. These Pakistani satellites are, in a way, filling the small gaps left in the already expansive Chinese satellite network. The orbits for these satellites are also chosen to ensure that regions of interest are monitored from multiple angles, range and clarity.
For instance, the PRSS-1 is Pakistan’s Earth-observation satellite, launched alongside PakTES-1A in July 2018. It is an electro-optical imaging payload, with two principal image products—panchromatic and multispectral.
Panchromatic imagery can distinguish objects or features roughly one metre across under suitable imaging conditions. Multispectral imagery captures information across different portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, helping identify vegetation, land-use patterns, water bodies and other surface features.
According to the Pakistani space agency, Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), PRSS-1 offers a four-day revisit capability anywhere on the globe. For example, if PRSS-1 captures an image of Delhi on Monday, it can capture another image of Delhi approximately four days later. It can do the same for locations elsewhere in the world. This allows scientists and authorities to monitor changes on the ground. PRSS-1 has ground stations in Islamabad and Karachi for receiving, processing, and archiving satellite imagery.
PAKSAT-MM1, launched in 2024, is a communications satellite, developed with Chinese assistance. It is designed to provide telecommunications services across Pakistan and surrounding regions. It carries payloads operating in four frequency bands: C-band for television broadcasting and communications, Ku-band for broadcasting, VSAT (very small aperture terminal) connectivity and mobile backhaul, Ka-band for high-speed broadband and high-throughput internet, and L-band for satellite-based augmentation services (SBAS), which can improve positioning and navigation accuracy.
PRSC-EO1, on the other hand, is a part of Pakistan’s newer remote-sensing satellite programme, which uses optical sensors to acquire images of the Earth’s surface.
All of these satellites received technological and launch support from China.
In 2022, Pakistan’s SUPARCO and the China Great Wall Industry Corporation (CGWIC)—a subsidiary of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC)—signed a multi-launch service agreement to provide Pakistan with a long-term arrangement to launch multiple satellites using China’s rockets and associated technical services.
Also read: Exclusive: 3 Chinese satellites stayed focused on Gujarat coast during Operation Sindoor
Complementing ground support
Digantara’s space surveillance report has also found Pakistan’s growing involvement in the Asia-Pacific Ground-Based Space Object Observation System Project (APOSOS) to be concerning.
APOSOS is a multinational space-surveillance network initiated under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization (APSCO), in which China plays a central role in its operation and data management. The project uses ground-based optical telescopes to observe and track objects in space, including satellites.
Curiously, Pakistan was one of the three countries where the first three observation nodes or stations of APOSOS were established. Each node is equipped with a 15-cm aperture optical telescope, and observation data from the different nodes is transmitted to a central facility at the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in China’s capital, Beijing. The other two stations are Peru and Iran.
Since Pakistan is not just a member of APOSOS, but the host of one of the facilities, it has gained a geographical advantage of getting access to observations from different parts of the world, which can be used to track satellites in orbit, including India’s space assets.
This is the third article in ThePrint’s exclusive three-part series examining China’s space surveillance moves.
(Edited by Ratan Priya)

title: What Indian States Lose With the End of Kurian Joseph Committee  - The Wire
description: An insider's account of the work that was done, the work that was left, and why both matter beyond one state.
author: R. Vanchinathan
content: I came to know that the high-level committee on Union-state relations had been dissolved only after seven in the evening on November 6. It was the start of a long weekend. By the time I left the State Guest House at Chepauk that night, my desk was empty. I worked there as a research officer since November 2025. I am writing this because people outside the committee may not fully know what was being done there, and what has now been stopped.The committee was set up in April 2025 by the then Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam government. Justice Kurian Joseph, former judge of the Supreme Court, was chairman, and K. Ashok Vardhan Shetty, a retired IAS officer, and Professor M. Naganathan were members. The government order gave it a very wide scope, but a specific and in-depth one. It had to review the provisions of the constitution and the laws and policies affecting Union-state relations “in all spheres”, look at how subjects moved into the Concurrent List could go back to the states, and recommend “utmost autonomy” for the states without prejudice to the unity of the country.Even the way we worked was laid down in a government order. For every subject, the research officers prepared a background note covering the Constituent Assembly debates, what had happened on that subject since 1950, the relevant Supreme Court judgments, what earlier commissions had said, and how other federations dealt with the same question. Apart from the elections and health chapters of Part I, my own share was mostly the comparative research, across eight countries from the United States and Canada to Germany, Switzerland and Brazil.Only after these notes were discussed did the committee settle on its recommendations.Why it matteredTo explain why this exercise was important, I turn to Tom Ginsburg and Aziz Huq. In How to Save a Constitutional Democracy, they write about two ways in which a democracy can be lost. One is authoritarian reversion, where constitutional rule is suspended openly and suddenly. The other, which they call constitutional retrogression, is slower. The Constitution is not set aside here. Its own procedures are used, one step at a time, to weaken the institutions that are meant to check power.India has gone through both since the Rajamannar Committee gave its report in 1971. The Emergency was an authoritarian reversion, though a temporary one. It lasted less than two years, but some of what was done then has stayed with us, including the 42nd Amendment that took education out of the State List.Also read: Why Did Vijay’s TVK Government Disband Tamil Nadu’s Kurian Joseph Committee on State Autonomy?What we have seen since 2014 is, in my reading, constitutional retrogression. Jammu and Kashmir was split and turned into Union territories, under Article 3 during President’s Rule, when it had no functioning Assembly. Governors have sat on Bills passed by elected Assemblies, sometimes for years. The Union has an effective veto in the GST Council. National entrance examinations now decide admissions to colleges that states built and pay for. All of this was done through legal means, which is why it is so hard to challenge. Taken together, they keep moving power towards the Union government. I believe this goes beyond turning India into a unitary country. It is pushing the country towards a fascist state, where one centre gives orders and the states are expected to follow. Scholars who would not use my word describe the same direction. In ‘One Nation,’ BJP, and the Future of Indian Federalism (India Review, 2020), Yamini Aiyar and Louise Tillin show how the BJP’s “One Nation” project joins a unitary, Hindu nationalist idea of India to a drive to centralise policy, even in areas where states once led. They also recall L.K. Advani telling his party in 1987 that the constitution was “federal in form but essentially unitary in content”.Between Rajamannar and now, the Union set up the Sarkaria Commission and, later, the Punchhi Commission. Both looked at Union-state relations seriously, but neither was willing to recommend structural changes to the constitution along the lines of state autonomy. The Kurian Joseph Committee was the first body after Rajamannar that looked at both these experiences and asked what in the constitution itself has to change so that they do not happen again. I would place it among the most important exercises on federalism since the constitution was adopted.What Part I saidPart I was given to the government on February 16 and later tabled in the Assembly. It has 10 chapters and roughly a hundred recommendations, and some of them would change the constitution in basic ways. It proposes that amendments affecting the states be ratified by two-thirds of the states, which together hold two-thirds of the population. It says no state should be divided, renamed or downgraded without its own consent. It suggests that governors be appointed from a panel approved by the state assembly, with time limits for acting on Bills and assent deemed to be given once those limits pass. On delimitation, the report works out that if the freeze on Lok Sabha seats is lifted, Tamil Nadu goes down from 39 seats to 29 while Bihar goes up from 40 to 50. On GST, it shows that even if every state votes the same way in the Council, they cannot reach the 75% needed for a decision unless the Union agrees.Before Part I went out, our team worked 97 days at a stretch, weekends included, often 12 hours or more a day. Every line was checked against its source. The response was wider than any of us had expected. Justice J. Chelameswar called the report timely and scholarly. The Hindu’s editorial said it convincingly dismantled the case for centralisation. Sitting judges of four high courts, a former election commissioner, a former Union finance secretary, two Union ministers from the BJP, and Karnataka’s Siddaramaiah wrote to the committee in appreciation.What was left undonePart II was about 60% done when we were shut down. It dealt with emergency provisions and President’s Rule, Union agencies like the CBI and NIA, Union-state financial, legislative and administrative relations, forests and environment, inter-state river waters, mines and minerals, transport, disaster management, and history, culture, arts and science. These are the subjects that decide how much real power a state has.Whether a state has the money to run its own schemes, and how far a union agency can walk into a state’s affairs, were questions for Part II. Part I was also written on the understanding that Part II would follow. The Governor chapter, for example, does not take up Article 356 in full, because that was kept for the chapter on emergency provisions. Without Part II, even Part I remains incomplete.The Law Commission argumentThe dissolution order says our work overlaps with that of the State Law Commission, and that our records should be handed over to it. I have read the order that created the Law Commission in May 1994. Its main job is to examine every law in force, starting with those made under British rule, and advise whether they still suit present conditions. Among a list of other duties, one clause asks it to “suggest ways and means for the inter-State Relations and Centre-State Relations”. That clause has been carried over each time the commission is reconstituted for three years. One clause in a general law-reform brief cannot be equated with a committee set up to go through the whole constitution, and the laws and policies under it, from the standpoint of state autonomy. That was our only job, and lawyers, economists, journalists and retired administrators worked together on it.The order also describes our committee as non-statutory. So is the law commission. It was created by a government order, the same way we were. And the existence of a law commission has never stopped governments from setting up a separate body on this subject. The Law Commission of India has been around since 1955, yet the Union-appointed Sarkaria in 1983 and Punchhi in 2007, because the question needed people who would work on nothing else.There is a practical problem too. While writing Part I, we spent a great deal of time making sure that no recommendation in one chapter contradicted another. For Part II, we were just as careful that nothing would clash with what Part I had already said. With about a hundred recommendations already out and 15 chapters still in progress, keeping all of it consistent needs people who know the whole report, not just a set of files.A new body will have to start almost from the beginning. It also bothers me that the work begun under a former Supreme Court judge is being given to a body headed by a former high court judge. I see it as a slight to Justice Kurian Joseph, and to the Supreme Court as an institution. The order only says that records be handed over. It does not say who will finish Part II, by when, or whether it will be published at all.How it endedAfter the new government came in, VCK minister Vanni Arasu said in the Assembly on May 13 that the committee should not be closed. We were then told we could carry on, with one condition. Our secretary and research officer, a former registrar of the University of Madras and an economist who had served on the State Planning Commission, could not continue, because the government had doubts about his political leanings. He left. After that, contracts began running out without renewal. The office assistants and the accountant were gone by the end of August. The translator’s contract was not renewed in October. The order that set us up asks for the final report in English and Tamil, so without the translator the Tamil version could not be done. Then came the order of November 6.The committee came under the Public Department, which is with the chief minister, and the government’s own order names the secretary of that department as our single point of contact. But when the dissolution was questioned, it was law minister C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar who spoke for the government, though his department had nothing to do with us. As early as September, there were news reports linking him to pressure Justice Kurian Joseph to step down. Sources inside the committee also named him as the one who pushed for the dissolution. Nirmal Kumar was in the Bharatiya Janata Party for years before he moved to the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and then to Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam. The only political leader to welcome the dissolution was Narayanan Thirupathy of the BJP. The chief minister himself has said nothing so far.What has been lostThe loss is not Tamil Nadu’s alone. Federal reform in this country has usually begun with one state doing the groundwork and others following. Siddaramaiah had already called on all states to come together on these questions. The next delimitation and the next Finance Commission are not far away, and Part II would have given the states much of what they need for both.The larger loss takes me back to Ginsburg and Huq. The Emergency was an open break, and it was undone in the open: voters threw out the government in 1977, and the 44th Amendment repaired much of the damage. Retrogression does not work like that. No single step looks like a breach, so there is never one clear moment to resist. Tarunabh Khaitan calls it “killing a constitution with a thousand cuts”, an assault that is gradual but systematic. He names the centrally-appointed Governor as one of the original design flaws that made those cuts possible, records a sharp fall in the independence of the Election Commission after 2014, and describes the downgrading of Jammu and Kashmir as, in effect, amending the Constitution by executive action.Part I of our report reads almost like a list of those cuts, with a remedy set against each. The chapter on elections proposed a selection panel for Election Commissioners in which the government of the day would no longer have the final say. The chapter on territorial integrity said no state could be broken up or downgraded without its own consent. The governor chapter set out to correct the very design flaw Khaitan points to. The delimitation chapter dealt with a cut that is still to come. None of these is a debate from the past. Every one of them is in the news today.A reversion can be voted out, as it was in 1977. Retrogression has to be answered in the Constitution itself, by changing the rules that make the cuts so easy to make. That was the work the committee was doing, and Part II was meant to finish it. Until now, constitutional retrogression in India has been driven from the Union. On November 6, it found an ally in a state government.R. Vanchinathan was a Research Officer with the High-Level Committee on Union-State Relations (Justice Kurian Joseph Committee), Government of Tamil Nadu.

title: Expelled for Writing on an ABVP Poster, Two Presidency University Students Refuse to Back Down - The Wire
description: Of the two, the former student who was barred from campus activities has refused to apologise. The current student has turned down the university’s offer of writing a supplementary exam.
author: Soumashree Sarkar
content: Kolkata: In October this year, Annie*, an undergraduate topper, was studying at the two-century-old Presidency University in Kolkata for her Masters, and working on a dissertation on how animals are taught violence. Olivia Banerjee, a UGC junior research fellow, was in the applications stage for a PhD on how caste and Hindutva thought has entered the carceral system. She had a Masters from Presidency University, where she had studied Sociology for her Bachelors as well. Her single mother is ailing, so Kolkata – and Presidency – was her first choice for a doctorate. By mid-November, Presidency University had ‘expelled’ both Annie and Olivia. Their crime was writing on and beside a poster of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP). The poster also had an image of Swami Vivekananda on it.The writing on the wallIn May this year, concerned at what would happen to the spirit of academic engagement if the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power – it did – the two had been active in setting up a collective called Rerooting the Field. The group was born out of the Sociology department and, according to Annie, aimed to democratise academic conversations and interrogate methods with which we study the world around us.As the BJP government settled into power, attacks on some of West Bengal’s most illustrious campuses like Jadavpur University (JU) and Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) by Hindutva supporters became frequent news. The collective began thinking of holding an event to protest against the assaults on campus across West Bengal, say the two. They conceptualised a cultural event, ‘Art in Solidarity’, for October 13. “There were 18 speakers for the event, mostly from Jadavpur University, SRFTI, independent gender activists and left-leaning, left-of-centre student organisations,” Olivia says. There was a mural showing scholar Rohith Vemula, who was driven to suicide by caste discrimination, and Chuni Kotal, a legendary Lodha anthropologist, which Olivia notes had been whitewashed ahead of a National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) visit to the campus. The organisers aimed to restore that mural at the October 13 event. Many others took up paintbrushes to paint other walls too. The walls of government institutions across West Bengal have often become canvases for political art and slogans. “I saw an ABVP recruitment drive poster, right beside the Arts library. I told Annie that I wanted to write something on that poster to register my dissent. Annie came along. She was just standing there, throughout the time when I was writing it. On the ABVP banner, I wrote, “Rapist, casteist,” and beside that, I wrote, “F*ck RSS.” Annie drew an arrow from the poster and I wrote, “Throw garbage here”,” Olivia says. A third student accompanied them but was not a part of this writing exercise. On the same day, a History assistant professor, Gourav Lama, posted on Facebook about the graffiti on campus. Lama, who tagged chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, BJP MP Samik Bhattacharya and BJP national executive committee member Anirban Ganguly, couched the graffiti as an insult to Swami Vivekananda. “I firmly condemn the defacement of Swamiji’s image, irrespective of who is responsible,” he wrote in the post (image below). This representation of the ABVP recruitment poster as an ‘image of Swami Vivekananda’, the two feel, triggered the chain of events that would lead to their eventual expulsion. “Lama did not go through any university avenues to voice his discomfort,” Olivia says. The Wire has emailed Lama for his side of things. This report will be updated if they respond.Incidentally, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS)-affiliated ABVP opened its Presidency University unit on October 13 itself, says Mridul Banik. Banik is a PhD scholar at Presidency University’s History department and the president of its ABVP chapter. October 13 is the same day on which the solidarity event was held, the students wrote on the poster, and Lama’s post appeared.“On October 14 we went to submit a deputation to the university authorities against the objectionable comments against a noteworthy historical figure,” Mridul says. Olivia and Annie say the ABVP’s march to the university on the day got violent, to the extent that police had to be called.Just before the Durga Puja holidays started, Olivia and Annie discovered from news reports that a disciplinary committee had been constituted to investigate their writing on the poster. During the holidays, on October 29, they say, a teacher of the Life Sciences who was close to the two of them – and whose identity the two of them have requested be protected – called them to the university’s second campus at Rajarhat. Once there, she indicated that she had been told that an apology was expected from them by university authorities. “She also said that she had learnt that I, despite being an alumnus, will be considered as an internal student so that the authorities can negotiate with government pressure,” says Olivia. Olivia says that she decided not to apologise. “I had done whatever I had done in good conscience,” she says.
